title: Lists
description:
Lists are a . . . list of elements. The list type is just a type surrounded by [ ]. A string is just a `[Char]`, and `++` is just the list concatenation operator.
There is one more special list operator: `:` (cons). The cons operator is used like this: `<elem> : <list>`. If we have a int list, x we could do `10 : x`.

---
## Function "pattern matching"
A function can have multiple definitions, and Haskell chooses the one that matches the input. Let's say that we have a function, isEmpty:
```haskell
isEmpty :: [Integer] -> Bool
```
Then we could do
```haskell
isEmpty [] = True;
isEmpty x = False;
```
We could also do this:
```haskell
isZero :: Integer -> Bool
isZero 0 = True
isZero x = False
```

---
## : in arguments
To get the first element in a list as a argument, you can do this;
```haskell
<funcname> (<name>:<list>) ....
```
Then `<name>` would be the first element, and `<list>` would be the rest. _The first element will not be part of the other list_
